## What this exercise is

Exercises 1--3 ran on data that shipped inside an R package. This one does not.
You will work with **real surveillance data** --- COVID-19 deaths in the 67
counties of Pennsylvania --- and assemble the analysis dataset yourself, the way
you would in a health department: a table of counts from one source, county
boundaries from another, and a join between them that has to be checked rather
than trusted.

From there the exercise follows the sequence of the last two weeks:

1. join and project the data;
2. compute crude rates, **expected counts**, and the **standardized mortality
   ratio (SMR)**;
3. map the SMR honestly --- which, for a ratio, is not the same as mapping a rate;
4. build a spatial weights matrix and ask, with **global Moran's I**, whether
   the SMRs are spatially structured or could plausibly be arranged at random.

It is worth 17.5 points and carries more weight than the first two exercises.
Start early: Part A is where most of the unexpected problems will be.

::: {.callout-important}

## The data

**Counts.** `pa_covid_deaths_2020.csv` is posted on Course Site. It is a
subset of the **Johns Hopkins University CSSE COVID-19 Data Repository**
(`time_series_covid19_deaths_US.csv`), the source behind the JHU dashboard that
was the most widely used COVID-19 tracker in the United States until the project
stopped updating in March 2023. The repository compiles counts reported by state
health departments --- here, the Pennsylvania Department of Health --- and
attributes deaths to the county of residence.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `UID`, `FIPS` | JHU identifier; county FIPS code |
| `Admin2` | County name |
| `Province_State` | State |
| `Population` | County population (U.S. Census Bureau 2019 estimate, as carried in the JHU file) |
| `deaths_2020` | Cumulative COVID-19 deaths reported through December 31, 2020 |

Cite the source in your document as: Dong, E., Du, H., & Gardner, L. (2020). An
interactive web-based dashboard to track COVID-19 in real time. *The Lancet
Infectious Diseases, 20*(5), 533--534, together with the repository URL:
<https://github.com/CSSEGISandData/COVID-19>.

**Boundaries.** County polygons come from the U.S. Census Bureau's
**cartographic boundary files**, downloaded inside your document with the
`tigris` package. Install it once, in the console --- `install.packages(c("tigris", "ggrepel"))`
--- not inside the document.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why 2020
Calendar year 2020 is the first pandemic year and the period before vaccines
were available. Treat the population as the population at risk for one year.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(leaflet)
library(spdep)
library(ggrepel)            # non-overlapping labels
library(tigris)
options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)   # download once, then reuse

covid <- read_csv("pa_covid_deaths_2020.csv")
pa    <- counties(state = "PA", cb = TRUE, year = 2020)
```

## Part A --- Assemble the dataset (3 points)

1. Inspect both objects. How many rows does `covid` have, and how many polygons
   does `pa` have? The two numbers differ. Find the rows responsible and say in
   one sentence what they are and why they cannot be mapped.

Covid has 69 rows, and pa has 67 rows. This is because there are 67 counties in PA, and the Covid dataset has two extra rows for "Out of PA" and "Unassigned." These can't be mapped because they don't have a boundary, they are not counties. 
   
   
2. Identify the column in each object that identifies a county. Show what the
   values look like in each, and say why they will not match as they stand.
   
The column that identifies a county in Covid is FIPS and is stored as a number, and the column in pa is GEOID stored as a character. These don't match because they are different variable types, and with the number, leading zeros are not preserved and could lead to mismatch when joining. 
   
3. Create a join key in `covid` that matches the one in `pa`, then **join the
   counts onto the polygons**. Show, with code, that every one of the 67 counties
   received a count --- do not just look at the map.
   
   
4. In two or three sentences: why join the table onto the polygons
   (`left_join(pa, covid)`) rather than the other way around, and what would an
   **inner** join have hidden from you if the key had been only partly wrong?
   
Joining covid on to pa allows for only the rows that are actual counties to be included, since pa is the one without the two extra rows. Also, since pa's identifying column is a character instead of a number, this will preserve leading zero's. The pa dataset contains all of the pa counties and nothing else, meaning that we should match to it rather than vice versa and end up with two extra item in the data. 

::: {.callout-tip}
Run the obvious join first, `left_join(pa, covid, by = c("GEOID" = "FIPS"))`,
and read the error message carefully. It tells you exactly what is wrong.
A FIPS code is an **identifier**, not a number: `42001` and `42001.0` are the same
number but not the same identifier, and a county such as `01001` in Alabama
would lose its leading zero.
:::

### Starting code

```{r}
#| label: a-starter

# A1
covid
pa
nrow(covid); nrow(pa)

# rows in the table with no polygon to go to (names are good enough to look)
anti_join(covid, st_drop_geometry(pa), by = c("Admin2" = "NAME"))

# A2 -- what type is each key?
str(covid$FIPS)
str(pa$GEOID)

# A3 -- a five-character, zero-padded text key
covid <- covid |>
  mutate(GEOID = sprintf("%05d", as.integer(FIPS)))

pa_covid <- pa |>
  left_join(covid, by = "GEOID")

# prove the join worked
sum(is.na(pa_covid$deaths_2020))
```

## Part B --- Coordinate reference system (1.5 points)

1. What CRS do the Census boundaries arrive in? Geographic or projected?

Since st_is_longlat(pa_covid) returns TRUE before transforming it, this means we are using a geographic CRS, as coordinates are expressed in longitude and latitude. 

2. Transform `pa_covid` to a **projected** CRS appropriate for the whole state,
   and state its EPSG code. Pennsylvania is split between two State Plane zones
   (North and South) and two UTM zones, so the obvious choices each cover only
   part of the state --- say what you chose and why it is acceptable for a
   statewide map.
   
After some research, I chose to use EPSG 5070 (NAD83) since google recommended it as the best option since it covers the entire continental US and not just one half of Pennsylvania. 

3. One sentence: which of the operations in this exercise actually depend on the
   projection, and which do not?
   
Making any kind of map or visually representing the counties would depend on the projection, but calculating SMR or joining datasets would not. 

### Starting code

```{r}
#| label: b-starter

st_crs(pa_covid)$input
st_is_longlat(pa_covid)

pa_covid <- st_transform(pa_covid, 5070)
st_is_longlat(pa_covid)
```

## Part C --- Counts, rates, expected counts, and the SMR (4.5 points)

1. Compute the **crude COVID-19 mortality rate per 100,000** for 2020 in every
   county. Report the three highest and three lowest.
   
Three highest: Mifflin, Northumberland, Bedford
Three lowest: Wayne, Forest, Greene
   
2. Make two quick static maps with `ggplot2`, placed side by side: the **number
   of deaths** as **proportional symbols**, and the **crude rate** as a
   choropleth with a sequential, colour-blind-safe palette. Both need a legend
   title with units. In two or three sentences: why is a count shown with
   symbols rather than a choropleth, which counties stand out on each map, and
   why do the two maps tell different stories?
   
 Proportional symbols is better for representing death counts versus rates as a chloropleth is usually used to communicate rate or the severity of an issue, but with raw count data, a chloropleth may misrepresent where the issue is the most "severe" and where intervention is most useful. Proportional symbols show burden with counts, and the chloropleth shows where the SMR is most severe meaning intervention is needed. 
   
3. Compute the **statewide reference rate** $r = \sum_i O_i / \sum_i P_i$, and
   from it the **expected count** in each county, $E_i = r \times P_i$. Show that
   $\sum_i E_i = \sum_i O_i$ and explain in one sentence why this must be so.
   
 The statewide reference rate is the total number of Covid deaths in PA divided by PA population. Then county expeted count is calculated by taking the statewide reference rate and multiplying it by that county's population. The sum of expected deaths equals the sum of observed deaths as they are both found using the actual deaths aggregated at the state level.   
  
  
4. Compute the **SMR**, $O_i / E_i$.
    a. Interpret the SMR of one county of your choice in a full sentence a
       county commissioner could understand.
       
  Lehigh county SMR = 1.088. Lehigh county has slightly more observed cases than what is expected, resulting in an SMR of 1.088. This number is not statistically significant as the CI contains 1, so there is not need for immediate intervention. 

    b. Divide each county's crude rate by the statewide rate and compare with the
       SMR. Explain why they are identical here, and what $E_i$ would have to
       take into account for the two to differ. *(This is where we are going
       later in the semester.)*

The two are similar because both calculate by comparing the county's mortality rate with the statewide rate, using only population to determine expected count. If expected count reflected demographics, meaning it changed depending on what percent of the population is 65+ or other features, it would change our calculations. 
      

5. Compute an exact **95% confidence interval** for every SMR (formula below).
   Compare the intervals for the two or three counties with the **fewest**
   deaths with those of the counties with the **highest** SMRs. In three or four
   sentences: what does this tell you about the extreme values on an SMR map?
   
The three counties with the fewest deaths have rather large confidence intervals, showing how SMR can be highly variable in counties with low counts. On the other hand, counties with the highest SMRs have smaller intervals that are well above one, confirming higher than usual observed counts. This shows that for extremely low population counts or in situations with high variability, SMR can be less accurate and have a wide confidence interval. 

::: {.callout-note}
## Where the confidence interval comes from
Treat the expected count $E$ as a fixed constant and the observed count as
Poisson, $O \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu)$ with $\mu = \text{SMR} \times E$. We first
find an exact 95% interval for $\mu$ and then divide both ends by $E$.

The lower bound $\mu_L$ is the value of $\mu$ at which observing $O$ **or more**
deaths has probability 0.025; the upper bound $\mu_U$ is the value at which
observing $O$ **or fewer** has probability 0.025. Because of the link between the
Poisson and chi-square distributions, both have a closed form:

$$
\mu_L = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\chi^2_{0.025,\;2O}, \qquad
\mu_U = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\chi^2_{0.975,\;2(O+1)} .
$$

Dividing by $E$ gives the interval for the SMR:

$$
\left[\ \frac{\chi^2_{0.025,\,2O}}{2E}\ ,\ \ \frac{\chi^2_{0.975,\,2(O+1)}}{2E}\ \right].
$$

The upper bound uses $2(O+1)$ degrees of freedom and the lower bound $2O$; that
asymmetry is what keeps the interval exact when counts are small. When $O = 0$
the lower bound is 0.

**Worked example.** A county with $O = 4$ and $E = 5.57$ has SMR $= 0.72$ and

```r
qchisq(0.025, 2 * 4)       / (2 * 5.57)   # 0.20
qchisq(0.975, 2 * (4 + 1)) / (2 * 5.57)   # 1.84
poisson.test(4, T = 5.57)$conf.int        # same interval: E acts as the "time base"
```

The familiar normal approximation, $\text{SMR} \times \exp(\pm 1.96/\sqrt{O})$,
works for counties with many deaths but breaks down for the smallest ones ---
which are exactly the counties this question is about --- and is undefined when
$O = 0$.
:::

### Starting code

```{r}
#| label: c-starter

# C1
pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(crude_rate = 100000 * deaths_2020 / Population)

# Three highest rates
pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(desc(crude_rate)) |>
  select(NAME, Population, deaths_2020, crude_rate) |>
  head(3)

# Three lowest rates
pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(crude_rate) |>
  select(NAME, Population, deaths_2020, crude_rate) |>
  head(3)


# C2 -- counts as proportional symbols
pts <- st_point_on_surface(pa_covid)        # one point inside each county

p_count <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = pa_covid, fill = "grey95", colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_sf(data = pts, aes(size = deaths_2020),
          shape = 21, fill = "firebrick", colour = "white", alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 14, name = "Deaths(count)") +   # area proportional to count
  labs(title = "Pennsylvania COVID-19 Deaths by County, 2020") +
  theme_void()

# rates as a choropleth

p_rate <- ggplot(pa_covid) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = crude_rate), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, name = "Deaths, crude rate") +
  labs(title = "Pennsylvania COVID-19 Deaths by County, 2020") +
  theme_void()

p_count + p_rate

# C3 -- one number for the whole state
r <- sum(pa_covid$deaths_2020) / sum(pa_covid$Population)
r * 100000                         # per 100,000

pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(E = r * Population)

sum(pa_covid$E); sum(pa_covid$deaths_2020)

# C4
pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(SMR = deaths_2020 / E)

pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(rate_ratio = (crude_rate / 100000) / r)

pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(NAME, crude_rate, rate_ratio, SMR) |>
  head(10)


# C5 -- exact Poisson interval
pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(SMR_lo = qchisq(0.025, 2 * deaths_2020) / (2 * E),
         SMR_hi = qchisq(0.975, 2 * (deaths_2020 + 1)) / (2 * E))

pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(deaths_2020) |>
  select(NAME, Population, deaths_2020, E, SMR, SMR_lo, SMR_hi) 

pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(SMR) |>
  select(NAME, Population, deaths_2020, E, SMR, SMR_lo, SMR_hi) 

```

## Part D --- Mapping a ratio (3.5 points)

In Exercise 1 a sequential palette was the right choice for a rate. An SMR is
different: it is a ratio with a **meaningful reference value of 1**, and it is
**multiplicative** --- an SMR of 2 is as far above expected as 0.5 is below it.

1. Map the SMR as an interactive **`leaflet`** map with a **diverging palette
   centred on 1** and **class breaks you set yourself**. Choose breaks that are
   symmetric on the ratio scale, and make the class around 1 read as "about as
   expected". Justify the palette and the breaks in three or four sentences.
   
I choose 4/5 - 1.25 (0.8-1.25) for the middle boundary as these are relatively close to 1 and when a SMR varies from 1 by this little, it is most likely not statistically significant. Since 1/2 is just as severe as 2, I put these as the second and second to last values (after 0 and infinity) as I felt that these should represent the most extreme colors, SMRs in these range are much more likely to be statistically significant. The palate goes from blue for lower SMRs to white for normal (values around 1) to red for high SMRs to show more cases then expected. Going from blue to white to red is appropriate to show a diverging scale with blue being "good" and red being "bad." 
   
2. Your SMR map meets the standards from Exercise 1 --- legend title with
   units or meaning, thin boundaries, colour-blind-safe palette --- and in
   addition:
    - a **source line** on the map naming the data and the year;
    - a **popup** for each county giving the observed and expected deaths, the
      SMR, and its 95% interval from C5. This is what makes an interactive map
      worth having: the reader can check how much evidence stands behind a
      colour.

::: {.callout-warning}
## `leaflet` wants longitude and latitude
Web maps are drawn on a Web Mercator basemap and expect coordinates in
**EPSG:4326**. Your `pa_covid` is now projected (Part B), so give `leaflet` a
transformed **copy**, `st_transform(pa_covid, 4326)`, and keep the projected
object for everything else. Handing it projected coordinates is the most common
reason for a blank `leaflet` map.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What earns full marks here
Breaks that follow from what an SMR *means*, not from the distribution of the
values. A student who can explain why 0.67 and 1.5 belong in the same break set
understands the variable.
:::

### Starting code

```{r}
#| label: d-starter

pa_wgs <- st_transform(pa_covid, 4326)      # leaflet needs lon/lat

# D1 -- breaks symmetric on the ratio scale: 1/x and x
brks <- c(0, 1/2, 2/3, 4/5, 5/4, 3/2, 2, Inf)

pal <- colorBin("RdBu", domain = pa_wgs$SMR, bins = brks,
                reverse = TRUE)             # red = high

leaflet(pa_wgs) |>
  addTiles() |>                               # OpenStreetMap basemap
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~pal(SMR), fillOpacity = 0.8,
    color = "white", weight = 0.6,          # thin boundaries
    label = ~NAME,                          # shown on hover
    popup = ~sprintf("<b>%s County</b><br>Observed: %d<br>Expected: %.1f<br>SMR: %.2f (95%% CI %.2f–%.2f)",
                     NAME, deaths_2020, E, SMR, SMR_lo, SMR_hi),
    highlightOptions = highlightOptions(weight = 2, color = "black",
                                        bringToFront = TRUE)
  ) |>
  addLegend(pal = pal, values = ~SMR, opacity = 0.8,
            title = "SMR (observed/expected)", labFormat = labelFormat(digits = 2)) |>
  addControl("Johns Hopkins University CSSE COVID-19 Data Repository (2020), US Census Bureau (2019)", position = "bottomleft")   # source line
```

::: {.callout-note}
A `leaflet` map is an HTML widget: it appears in the rendered page on your
GitHub Pages site, which is where I grade it. It will not appear in a PDF.
:::

## Part E --- Spatial weights and global Moran's I (4 points)

1. Build a **queen contiguity** neighbour list. Report the average number of
   neighbours, the smallest and largest, and whether any county has none.
   
The average number of neighbors is 5.1, smallest is 2 links, largest is 9 links, no county has 0 links. 
   
2. Convert it to **row-standardized** spatial weights. One sentence: what does
   row standardization do to a county's neighbours, and what does the spatial
   lag of the SMR then represent?
   
Row-standardized spatial weights weighs each county similarly, meaning that the nearest neighbor value/spatial lag just becomes an average of all the counties that that county touches.    
   
3. Compute **global Moran's I** for the SMR by permutation with `moran.mc()`
   (999 simulations; set a seed), and plot the permutation distribution with the
   observed value marked. Report $I$, its expectation under the null hypothesis,
   $-1/(n-1)$, and the $p$-value. In three or four sentences: what exactly is the
   null hypothesis, how does the simulation test it, and is there a spatial
   signal in the SMRs?
   
 Our observed Moran's I value is 0.289 with an expected value of -0.015. The null hypothesis claims that there is no observed autocorrelation. The simulation tests this by "shuffling" the SMR value across the PA counties 999 times to determine how extreme our value is/if it would occur by chance, plotting that with the observed shuffling. Because of a p-value of 0.001, we can reject the null and say that there is an observed spatial signal in the SMRs. 
   
4. Draw the **Moran scatterplot**, with every county labelled and coloured by
   quadrant. Name two or three counties in the high--high quadrant and two or
   three in the low--low quadrant, say in one sentence what the slope of the fitted line is, and say in
   one sentence what Moran's I does **not** tell you about these counties.
   
Northumberland and Mifflin have by far the two highest SMR values, and Wayne, Forest, and Greene have the lowest. The slope of the fitted line is positively increasing, representing a spatial association between counties and their neighbors. However, Moran's I does not tell us why or whether this slope is significant. 

### Starting code

```{r}
#| label: e-starter

# E1
nb <- poly2nb(pa_covid, queen = TRUE)
summary(nb)

# E2
lw <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W")

# E3 -- shuffle the SMRs across counties 999 times
set.seed(374)
mc <- moran.mc(pa_covid$SMR, lw, nsim = 999)
mc

-1 / (nrow(pa_covid) - 1)          # expectation under the null

hist(mc$res, breaks = 40, main = "Permutation distribution of I", xlab = "I")
abline(v = mc$statistic, col = "red", lwd = 2)

# E4 -- moran.plot() labels only influential points; build it in ggplot2
mp_df <- pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(lag_SMR = lag.listw(lw, SMR),          # mean SMR of neighbours
         quad = case_when(
           SMR >= mean(SMR) & lag_SMR >= mean(SMR) ~ "High-High",
           SMR <  mean(SMR) & lag_SMR <  mean(SMR) ~ "Low-Low",
           SMR >= mean(SMR) & lag_SMR <  mean(SMR) ~ "High-Low",
           TRUE                                    ~ "Low-High"))

ggplot(mp_df, aes(SMR, lag_SMR)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(mp_df$SMR), linetype = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(mp_df$SMR), linetype = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = quad), size = 2) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = NAME), size = 2.6, max.overlaps = Inf) +   # every county
  labs(x = "SMR", y = "Neighbors Average", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

table(mp_df$quad)
```
